chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from his brother Al-'Ala', from Ismail ibn Al-Hasan Al-Mutabbib (the physician) who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I am a man from the Arabs, and I have insight into medicine, and my medicine is Arab medicine, and I do not take gifts for it.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem.'
I said, 'We bleed the wound and cauterize it with fire.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem.'
I said, 'And we give these toxins, Al-Asmahiqun and Al-Ghariqun.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem.'
I said, 'Sometimes he (the patient) dies.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Even if he dies.'
I said, 'We give him Al-Nabidh (intoxicating drink).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no healing in the prohibited.'

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) complained, so Ayesha said to him, 'You have pleurisy.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'I am more honorable to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that He would test me with pleurisy.'
He (peace be upon him) said, 'So he ordered that he be cupped with sabr (a type of herb or method).'

key_terms.النَّبِيذَ: Al-Nabidh (fermented drink, often used as a medicinal example here)
key_terms.ذَاتُ الْجَنْبِ: Pleurisy (inflammation of the lining of the lungs)
key_terms.نَبْطُ الْجُرْحَ: To bleed a wound (letting blood flow)

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic rulings on bleeding, cauterization, and medicinal intoxicants?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (as) validates traditional Arab medical practices such as cupping, cauterization, and administering specific toxins, confirming their permissibility even if they result in death, thereby establishing the principle of *'illaj'* (treatment) overriding minor prohibitions. The Imam clarifies that while intoxicants like *Nabidh* are used medicinally, the core principle remains that 'there is no healing in the prohibited,' a concept supported by the Prophet’s own treatment of pleurisy with honey, which is cited to justify seeking cure through permissible means. This narration highlights the Shia scholarly view that medical necessity permits the use of otherwise restricted substances, provided the primary intent is healing rather than intoxication.
